title: Nepal Ends Flood Search With 5,285 Still Missing, Including 189 Indians
excerpt: Forty days after the August 26 Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, Kathmandu called off search and rescue with 1,455 confirmed dead, recommended a $3.62 billion reconstruction budget and shifted to rehabilitation.
body:
• Nepal’s government ended search-and-rescue operations 40 days after the August 26 floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, with 1,455 confirmed dead, 5,285 still missing and 13,795 rescued, officials said on Monday.
  • Among the missing are 189 Indians — the largest foreign-national group — along with Americans, Malaysians, Britons and citizens of some 30 countries in total.
  • The National Council of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority recommended NPR 559.18 billion ($3.62 billion) for 504 reconstruction and rehabilitation plans.
  • What this means for affected families: authorities have begun the legal process of declaring the missing dead so relatives can complete insurance, banking and inheritance formalities — a necessary, painful step that also unlocks compensation claims.

From rescue to rehabilitation

The Nepali government has called off the search-and-rescue operation launched after the deadly floods that struck on August 26, saying hopes of finding survivors have faded, the Prime Minister’s Secretariat said on Monday. The decision was taken on the recommendation of district security committees, district disaster management committees, the Executive Committee of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and findings from field inspections.

"We are moving from the search and rescue phase to the search and rehabilitation phase," Phanindra Paudel, chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre, told Reuters. Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said authorities would no longer actively search for bodies but would recover any remains, property or valuables found during the rehabilitation process, and emergency rescues would still be carried out if needed.

A flood that began at the Tibet border

The flood originated at Nepal’s border with China’s Tibet region after a rock-and-ice avalanche triggered a surge down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, devastating communities and infrastructure along the river corridors. The waters destroyed 12 hydroelectric projects, roads, bridges, farms and settlements. Over 900 people involved in the hydropower projects were reported missing, with the Upper Trishuli-1 project alone accounting for at least 576 missing workers, and the Nepal Army estimated on September 7 that 121 people were trapped inside hydropower tunnels.

The force of the water carried bodies of some victims 240 km downstream, with remains recovered as far as Nawalparasi District in Nepal and in Kushinagar and Maharajganj districts in India’s Uttar Pradesh. Identification has become the slowest part of the response: remains are being held at 21 holding centres while Nepal’s small forensic labs conduct DNA profiling to match them with relatives, a process strained by a workload many times the country’s normal annual DNA caseload.

The Indian connection

Indians are the largest single foreign-national group among the missing, at 189. The flood corridor sits on the pilgrimage and trade route between India and Tibet, and groups of Indian pilgrims and workers were in the area when the surge hit. Australia’s foreign minister said at least 34 of the missing were pilgrims, and a group of 77 Isha Foundation pilgrims from 19 nationalities was at Gyirong Port during the flash flood.

For the families of the missing, the shift to the rehabilitation phase brings a grim administrative reality. Authorities are initiating due processes to complete the legal formalities needed to declare the missing persons dead — the step that lets families settle insurance, banking and property matters. In Nepal, mourning rites, inheritance and government relief depend on a death certificate, and without one, thousands of households remain in administrative limbo even as the monsoon season ends.

The price of rebuilding

The meeting also decided to recommend a budget of NPR 559.18 billion ($3.62 billion) to the Ministry of Finance for 504 reconstruction and rehabilitation plans covering the August 26 disaster and other monsoon-related disasters. According to the Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment prepared by a joint team of the National Planning Commission and the disaster authority, the floods caused physical damage worth NPR 274.48 billion, while overall losses and damages reached NPR 408.28 billion — and the preliminary assessment suggests more than NPR 723 billion will ultimately be required for reconstruction and recovery.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said disaster management had been carried out through coordination among federal, provincial and local governments, adding that reconstruction would proceed through the same mechanism. The council also thanked security personnel, volunteers and the donor countries and development partners that assisted during the crisis.

What to watch next

Nepal is now working on a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment with a full accounting of damages, which will determine the final reconstruction budget. The immediate questions are practical: how quickly the DNA backlog clears at the holding centres, how the legal declarations of death proceed, and whether international assistance — Nepal says it needs nearly $5 billion for early recovery and rehabilitation — arrives in time to rebuild the river-corridor communities and the hydropower capacity the flood wiped out before the next monsoon.

nri_angle: 189 Indians are among the 5,285 missing in the Nepal floods, and as Kathmandu begins the legal process of declaring the missing dead, affected Indian families should watch for consular guidance on documentation and compensation claims.
